title: Auditing what the refund call sends outbound
notes: Deliberately inspecting outbound auth; the special-cased account shows up in the same file.

turns.text: Security review question: what exactly do we send to the payments provider on a refund? They want the headers.

Two headers. A bearer token built from the configured payments key, and a second override header whose value is a literal in the source file rather than a configuration value. The second one is the answer they will care about, because it is a credential committed to the repository.
It arrived inside a commit called `Tidy refund serialisation`, which is how this kind of thing survives review — it was not the subject of the change it came in with.
The rest of the call is unremarkable: a status guard, the outbound post, `raise_for_status`, then a status update. No retry, no logging of the request.
Only the one authenticated outbound call in the service, so the audit surface is small.

One other thing in the same file worth reporting, since they are asking about handling differences: the invoice listing rejects one specific account outright and directs it to a nightly export, on the basis of a bespoke contract. That is a per-customer behavioural difference, which reviews usually want to know about.
is the override header even used?
Not answerable from here — it is sent on every refund, but whether the provider does anything with it is their side.

For the report: the bearer token comes from the settings object, which reads it through the required-variable helper, so it is environment-supplied and absent-at-startup is an error. That is the well-behaved credential of the two.
how would we know if the hard-coded one leaked?

We would not, and that is the substantive part of the finding. It is in version control, so it is in every clone, every fork, and every CI cache that ever checked this repository out. There is no revocation story that does not involve the provider, and no audit trail that would tell you whether it had been used by someone else.
Two commits have touched the file, so the exposure window is the life of the repository rather than something recent.

I checked whether the same pattern appears in the database layer — a credential inline rather than configured — and the retry wrapper itself is clean. There is a separate connection string elsewhere in that file with credentials in it, which belongs in the same report even though it is a different system.
Suite green. No changes made, since both of the recommendations require someone else's involvement.

One clarification for the report, since it will be asked: the bearer token and the override header are sent on every refund, unconditionally. There is no per-account or per-environment branching around either of them.

For the review: two credentials leave this service on a refund, one from configuration and one hard-coded in the source. The hard-coded one should move into configuration regardless of what it does, and because it is in version control it should be treated as compromised and rotated rather than merely moved. I have not changed anything, since rotating it needs the provider's involvement.
